content.text:
Fixed! The issue was floating-point arithmetic: when converting a decimal like `39.95` to cents by multiplying by 100, JavaScript's floating-point math produces `3995.0000000000005` instead of exactly `3995`, which failed the integer check.

I updated both `parseEuros()` and `cellCents()` functions in `src/money.js` to use `Math.round()` when converting to cents. This properly handles the floating-point imprecision and ensures all prices (including 39.95, 12.99, 10.99, etc.) work correctly.

input.command:
git add src/money.js && git commit -m "Fix floating-point precision in price-to-cents conversion

Use Math.round() instead of direct multiplication to handle floating-point
imprecision when converting decimal prices to whole cents. This fixes the
error when adding prices like 39.95 that don't convert exactly.

Fixes: price must be whole cents, zero or more (got 3995.0000000000005)
Co-Authored-By: Claude Haiku 4.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>"

I found the issue — I needed to fix the floating-point rounding in **two** places:

1. `src/money.js`: `parseEuros()` function
2. `src/locale.js`: `decimalCommaToCents()` function (for European decimal comma format)

Both had the same floating-point precision problem. Now it works for both US format (39.95) and European format (39,95):

This fixes the error when adding prices like 39.95 that don't convert exactly.
